name: Lydia Ames
home: the streets inland from Pier Beach
life: “I hate valuing instruments whose cases are worth more than my rent.” People around the courtyard by Ferry Street Rooms know Lydia by a small Friday habit. Lydia prefers the bench where the sound of the shop door reaches before the visitor does.
voice: I sold the trumpet with a practice mute. The mute is still on my shelf and so is the child's name.
appearance: Lydia has a broad nose and a deep dimple on one cheek. Look for salt-and-pepper curls. On an ordinary day, the familiar outfit is a narrow-striped sweater with a pocket notebook shaped by years of sitting on it. In conversation Lydia gathers both sleeves neatly before settling in.
personality: Lydia finds it easier to own up to a mistake than to accept praise. The worse the mistake, the more precise the account of exactly when it happened.
agenda: To return the practice mute with its original owner's name.
family: Lionel Wu is Lydia’s stepsibling. A relative let everybody believe a favorite tune was a folk song. Only later did the family find the melody in a book with a relative's real name under it. Lydia is quite capable of keeping a harmless secret for years. Asked about *A last ship together*, Lionel says, “I beat them at dominoes as a teenager. I want one last game with both clocks still ticking on company time.”
connections: Frank Hull. They compare the player's receipt with the mute still on the pawn counter. Also in the story is Clyde Darzi (brass repairer).

reactions.situation: A neighbor demands the trumpet stop playing
reactions.response: Lydia asks the player and the neighbor to choose a practice time they can both live with.
